searches.note: Twenty two searches of twenty eight, six unspent. Nine were restricted to a house's own domain (houseofarras.com.au, jansz.com.au twice, kreglingerwineestates.com twice, tolpuddlevineyard.com twice, domaine-a.com.au once; one restricted search also took in Decanter and Wine Companion) and are read as primary through their summaries; others blocked the house and the author's main sources so the second source would be independent. No WebFetch was tried. Counts by record include the shared searches (La Provence and Moorilla for Pipers Brook).

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: founding, people and dates, grapes, sites, making, ageing, serving, label words, every beat of the story, cards and questions; then the house rules.
Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was in one source only, or none, it was cut or said with less.
Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Campbell Mattinson, Tyson Stelzer) are cited neither in the fragment nor here as a second source.

The 1988 start: Wine Companion and Decanter date a visit by the winemaker in 1988, before he joined Hardys in the early 1990s. Changed.
The name: a word for a rich tapestry by World of Fine Wine and Wine Companion; the think tank in none. Cut.
The first release: 1999 by World of Fine Wine and Wine in Tasmania. Changed from the end of the decade.
Tirage, blend and dosage: the house's own pages for 2009, 2015, 2016 and 2017 (about two thirds Chardonnay, six to nine years, low dosage). Sound with the years set right.
The sale of 2023 to Handpicked with the Bay of Fires winery and cellar door: Inside FMCG, Drinks Trade, Winetitles, Wine Companion. Sound.
changes: story: the start was a winemaker of the Hardy company beginning a search in 1988; now a visit to Tasmania in 1988 by a sparkling winemaker who joined Hardys in the early 1990s (Wine Companion, Decanter: in 1988 he was not yet at Hardys).
story: the internal think tank that named the house cut; in no source this check read (Decanter, Wine Companion, World of Fine Wine, Wine in Tasmania).

story: the first Grand Vintage of 1995 reaching the market at the end of the decade; now the first Arras wine, of the 1995 harvest, that grew into the Grand Vintage, released in 1999 (World of Fine Wine, Wine in Tasmania).

Kreglinger in 2000 or 2001: Winestate, wine-pages and Young Gun of Wine. Sound; the de Moor line cut.

The Alsace model: the house's notes for 2001 and 2002. Sound.
The opening on Moorilla: La Provence of 1956 at Lalla (Wine Companion, Young Gun of Wine) and Moorilla of 1958 (Wikipedia). Changed.
changes: story: modern Tasmanian wine began in the south with Moorilla in 1958; now the 1950s, with La Provence at Lalla in the north in 1956 and Moorilla near Hobart in 1958 (Wine Companion's Providence page, Young Gun of Wine, Wikipedia: Moorilla Estate). The old line was wrong: the first modern vineyard was in the north.

story: the ground chosen for likeness to Champagne and Alsace and the aim to ripen three grapes cut to the house's own claim, a terroir that recalls the cool regions of France; the cornerstone line and the wine many guests first met cut as unsourced.

story: the de Moor family of Launceston has run it since cut (volatile, and Kreglinger is a Belgian family company whose chief executive moved to Launceston in 2002); now Kreglinger, a Belgian family trading company, and the estate trading as Kreglinger Wine Estates.
story: no oak in the closing line cut, in no source read; now close planted vines.

The making: the house's 2017, 2020 and 2025 pages (whole berries with whole bunches, about half in 2025 and forty per cent before, ten months in French oak about a third new, up to twelve years). Sound; gently plunged cut.

George Loveless: born 1797, died 1874, arrived at Hobart on 4 September 1834 by the convict record, set to work on the domain farm at New Town (Wikipedia), sailed on 30 January 1837. The Richmond link cut.
changes: story: by the vineyard's account Loveless served part of his sentence on a property near Richmond that became the vineyard; cut, and now he was set to work as a shepherd and stock keeper on the government's domain farm at New Town (Wikipedia, with the ADB as the author read it). The house's claim stands against two accounts of his assignment and was taken out, since a wrong fact is worse than a missing one.

The Stoney Vineyard of 1973 is called the valley's first commercial vineyard and its oldest by two sources in this check (Legend Australia, Coal River Valley Tasmania); the story still says only early in the valley's modern wine history, which the integrator may sharpen.

swaps.why: The author proposed no swap. The Pipers Brook pick, kept by the author with a note, is upheld: the house's notes model the Riesling on Alsace and no source of this check named another single flagship; the still wines carry the Pipers Brook name.

rules: No living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile (the de Moor line and the estate's owner as a present claim cut), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash: read across all five records after the edits. The note on still in the Pipers Brook trap is the still wine, kept.

The region record calls Tasmania the country's premier source of traditional method sparkling wine, a ranking. Reported, not edited.
The library gives no founding year for p-house-of-arras; 1995 is in four sources of this check and agrees with the region's producers line.
